solutionSteps: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Irrational rotation is}\\\textnormal{equidistributed by the}\\\textnormal{geometric-sum Weyl test.}\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: For every nonzero integer h, exp(2pi i h sqrt(2)) differs from one. The finite geometric sum of its first N powers has bounded numerator, so its average tends to zero.

Weyl criterion therefore makes {k sqrt(2)} uniformly distributed on [0,1]. The function q(t)=t{t+a} is bounded and has only one discontinuity, hence is Riemann integrable and its orbit averages converge to its integral.
For 0<=t<1-a, q=t(t+a); for 1-a<=t<1, q=t(t+a-1). Integrating the two quadratics yields 1/3-a/2+a^2/2.

analyticCertificate: For every integer N>=0, sin((2N+1)x)/sin x=1+2 sum_(j=1)^N cos(2jx), with continuous endpoint values. Its integral on0..pi is pi.
The kernel is invariant under x->pi-x. For f=x^m, reflection shows the integral of its endpoint-interpolating line ell(x)=pi^(m-1)x equals pi^(m+1)/2.
The polynomial h=f-ell vanishes at both endpoints. Hence g=h/sin x extends to a continuously differentiable function on the closed interval.
The residual is integral g(x)sin((2N+1)x)dx. Integration by parts bounds it by (|g(0)|+|g(pi)|+integral|g prime|)/(2N+1), which tends to zero.

solutionSteps: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Its n+1 alternating extrema}\\\textnormal{force every monic competitor}\\\textnormal{to have at least this maximum.}\end{gathered}
statement: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Let P be all real polynomials}\\\textnormal{of degree n with leading}\\\textnormal{coefficient one.}\\M_n=\inf_{p\in P}\max_{|x|\le 2}|p(x)|\\\lim_{n\to\infty}M_n^{1/n}\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: Define T_n(cos theta)=cos(n theta). Its recurrence implies leading coefficient2^(n-1) for n>=1, so q_n(x)=m^n2^(1-n)T_n(x/m) is monic.
On[-m,m], its maximum absolute value is C_n=m^n2^(1-n), attained with alternating signs at the n+1 points m cos(jpi/n).

If another monic degree-n polynomial had maximum below C_n, subtracting q_n would produce alternating nonzero signs at those points, hence at least n distinct roots. Its degree is at most n-1, a contradiction.
Thus the infimum is exactly C_n and is attained. Taking nth roots gives m/2 times2^(1/n), tending to m/2.

statement: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Let P be all real polynomials}\\\textnormal{of degree n with leading}\\\textnormal{coefficient one.}\\M_n=\inf_{p\in P}\max_{|x|\le 7}|p(x)|\\\lim_{n\to\infty}M_n^{1/n}\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: Define T_n(cos theta)=cos(n theta). Its recurrence implies leading coefficient2^(n-1) for n>=1, so q_n(x)=m^n2^(1-n)T_n(x/m) is monic.
On[-m,m], its maximum absolute value is C_n=m^n2^(1-n), attained with alternating signs at the n+1 points m cos(jpi/n).

If another monic degree-n polynomial had maximum below C_n, subtracting q_n would produce alternating nonzero signs at those points, hence at least n distinct roots. Its degree is at most n-1, a contradiction.
Thus the infimum is exactly C_n and is attained. Taking nth roots gives m/2 times2^(1/n), tending to m/2.

solutionSteps: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Use fixed odd and even}\\\textnormal{Bonferroni truncations before}\\\textnormal{taking the limit.}\end{gathered}
statement: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Throw balls independently}\\\textnormal{and uniformly into n boxes.}\\\textnormal{The number of throws is}\\r_n=\lfloor n\log n+n\log 2\rfloor\\p_n=\Pr(\textnormal{every box is occupied})\\\lim_{n\to\infty}p_n\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: For n boxes and r_n=floor(n log n+n log m) independent uniform throws, any specified j boxes are all empty with probability(1-j/n)^r_n.

For each fixed nonnegative j, C(n,j)(1-j/n)^r_n tends to m^-j/j!: expand log(1-j/n)=-j/n+O(n^-2), and use C(n,j)~n^j/j!. The floor changes the exponent by less than one and hence changes the factor by a ratio tending to one.
Bonferroni inequalities bound the no-empty-box probability between its finite inclusion-exclusion truncations of odd and even orders. First send n to infinity with truncation order fixed.
Then send the truncation order to infinity. Both limiting truncations converge to sum(-1)^j/(m^j j!)=exp(-1/m). No exchange with an n-dependent infinite alternating sum has been assumed.

solutionSteps: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{By determinant multilinearity,}\\\textnormal{the coefficient of x squared}\\\textnormal{is the sum of principal minors}\\\textnormal{obtained by deleting two}\\\textnormal{vertices.}\end{gathered}
\begin{gathered}\textnormal{A path block of length k with}\\\textnormal{diagonal 2 and adjacent -1 has}\\\textnormal{determinant k+1, from}\\D_k=2D_{k-1}-D_{k-2},\\D_0=1,\ D_1=2.\end{gathered}
\begin{gathered}\textnormal{Deleting vertices at cyclic}\\\textnormal{distance r leaves path lengths}\\\textnormal{r-1 and n-r-1; the minor}\\\textnormal{equals r(n-r).}\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: Multilinearity in columns selects either the old column or x times its coordinate vector. Selecting two coordinate columns leaves the corresponding principal minor with positive sign; thus the x squared coefficient is their sum. Every unordered vertex pair is counted twice by the n starting vertices and distances 1,...,n-1, including antipodal pairs. Removing the pair splits the cycle into two path blocks, with an empty block assigned determinant one. Their exact recurrence gives product r(n-r), and summing r and r squared yields the displayed formula.

solutionSteps: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{The trigonometric factor}\\\textnormal{alternates between sine and}\\\textnormal{cosine, with coefficient 1 or}\\\textnormal{-1. Induction follows by}\\\textnormal{differentiating the phase.}\end{gathered}

\begin{gathered}\textnormal{Thus all these derivatives at}\\\textnormal{zero exist and equal zero.}\\\textnormal{Through order m the punctured}\\\textnormal{derivatives also tend to zero.}\end{gathered}

\begin{gathered}\textnormal{At order m+1, a nonzero sine}\\\textnormal{or cosine term has constant}\\\textnormal{amplitude. Suitable sequences}\\\textnormal{make it approach 1 and -1, so}\\\textnormal{this derivative is not}\\\textnormal{continuous; dividing it by x}\\\textnormal{also prevents the next}\\\textnormal{derivative from existing.}\end{gathered}
statement: \begin{gathered}f(x)=\begin{cases}x^{10}\sin(1/x),&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0.\end{cases}\\\textnormal{Find (r,s), where r is the}\\\textnormal{greatest integer for which f}\\\textnormal{has an rth derivative at 0,}\\\textnormal{and s is the greatest integer}\\\textnormal{for which all derivatives}\\\textnormal{through order s are continuous}\\\textnormal{on a neighborhood of 0.}\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: Write each punctured derivative as A_k(x)sin(1/x)+B_k(x)cos(1/x). The recurrence A_(k+1)=A_k prime+B_k/x squared, B_(k+1)=B_k prime-A_k/x squared shows its smallest power is 2m+2-2k, with coefficient vector cycling (1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0),(0,1). All other terms have at least one higher power. For k<=m+1, the preceding derivative divided by x is O(|x|^(2m+3-2k)), which tends to zero, proving the derivative at zero inductively. For k<=m, the punctured derivative tends to zero, proving continuity. At k=m+1, choose positive sequences whose reciprocal phase makes the leading sine/cosine equal 1 and -1; the O(x) remainder vanishes. Hence this derivative is discontinuous. Along a sequence with leading value 1, its difference quotient at zero is unbounded, so derivative m+2 does not exist.

\begin{gathered}\textnormal{At order m+1, a nonzero sine}\\\textnormal{or cosine term has constant}\\\textnormal{amplitude. Suitable sequences}\\\textnormal{make it approach 1 and -1, so}\\\textnormal{this derivative is not}\\\textnormal{continuous; dividing it by x}\\\textnormal{also prevents the next}\\\textnormal{derivative from existing.}\end{gathered}
statement: \begin{gathered}f(x)=\begin{cases}x^{22}\sin(1/x),&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0.\end{cases}\\\textnormal{Find (r,s), where r is the}\\\textnormal{greatest integer for which f}\\\textnormal{has an rth derivative at 0,}\\\textnormal{and s is the greatest integer}\\\textnormal{for which all derivatives}\\\textnormal{through order s are continuous}\\\textnormal{on a neighborhood of 0.}\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: Write each punctured derivative as A_k(x)sin(1/x)+B_k(x)cos(1/x). The recurrence A_(k+1)=A_k prime+B_k/x squared, B_(k+1)=B_k prime-A_k/x squared shows its smallest power is 2m+2-2k, with coefficient vector cycling (1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0),(0,1). All other terms have at least one higher power. For k<=m+1, the preceding derivative divided by x is O(|x|^(2m+3-2k)), which tends to zero, proving the derivative at zero inductively. For k<=m, the punctured derivative tends to zero, proving continuity. At k=m+1, choose positive sequences whose reciprocal phase makes the leading sine/cosine equal 1 and -1; the O(x) remainder vanishes. Hence this derivative is discontinuous. Along a sequence with leading value 1, its difference quotient at zero is unbounded, so derivative m+2 does not exist.
